title: Every one had a name
hookLine: Yad Vashem gathers the name of every victim it can

cards: On Yom HaShoah, Israel's day of Holocaust remembrance, people step up to microphones in the Knesset, in schools, in synagogues, and read names aloud. One name. Then another.
Then the next. A grandmother. A cousin no one else remembers.
A child. Sometimes a reader adds a town, or a word about who the person was. The reading doesn't summarize or round anything off.
It just keeps going, one person at a time.

teach.b: Israel's Holocaust memorial takes its name from the prophet Isaiah.
There, God speaks to people who feared they would leave no children to carry their name, and promises them, in the Hebrew, a yad vashem: a monument and a memorial, literally a hand and a name.
The verse goes on: "I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off." Yad Vashem has spent its life gathering names.
One of its tools is plain: the Page of Testimony, a single sheet for a single person.
A relative or a friend writes down a name, a town, the names of parents, a job, what is known about how they died, and sometimes attaches a photograph.
The pages are kept in the Hall of Names, and the gathering goes on, because some names are still missing. The Israeli poet Zelda wrote a poem about this.

In paraphrase: every person has a name, given by God, by parents, by the way they stood and smiled, by the work they did, by the people who loved them. The name-reading ceremonies take their title from it.
Now look back at this week. Fighters in the Warsaw ghetto. The Trocmés, Chiune Sugihara, Irena Sendler.
Hannah Senesh. Soldiers at the gates, and the people they found. Witnesses who told.
Survivors who prayed, or argued, or stopped. All of it comes down to persons. Not a number.

how: On Yom HaShoah, communities in Israel and elsewhere hold name-reading ceremonies, and families fill in Pages of Testimony at Yad Vashem for relatives who were murdered.

games.q: you're asked to fill in a Page of Testimony for a great-aunt. you know only her first name and her town. what do you do?
o: leave it, since you don't know enough.
games.why: pages are filled in by relatives and friends with what they know. a name and a town keep a person from being lost.

practice: Choose one name, from this week, like Hannah Senesh or Irena Sendler, or from your own family, and say it out loud, slowly, once.

Then sit with it: not a statistic or a category, but a person who answered to that name when someone called it across a room. If you pray, hold that name in your prayer; if not, let it stay in the air of the room with you.
